Bug_Title: Back references in regular expressions should only refer to capturing groups that are matched before the reference
Bug_Details:
When a back reference in a regex refers to a capturing group that hasn’t been defined yet (or at all), it can never be matched. Named back
references throw a PatternSyntaxException in that case; numeric back references fail silently when they can’t match, simply making the
match fail.
When the group is defined before the back reference but on a different control path (like in (.)|\1 for example), this also leads to a
situation where the back reference can never match.
Noncompliant code example
Pattern.compile("\\1(.)"); // Noncompliant, group 1 is defined after the back reference
Pattern.compile("(.)\\2"); // Noncompliant, group 2 isn't defined at all
Pattern.compile("(.)|\\1"); // Noncompliant, group 1 and the back reference are in different branches
Pattern.compile("(?<x>.)|\\k<x>"); // Noncompliant, group x and the back reference are in different branches
Compliant solution
Pattern.compile("(.)\\1");
Pattern.compile("(?<x>.)\\k<x>");
Bug_Explanation: The code demonstrates the incorrect use of back references in regular expressions. In pattern1, \1 refers to a capturing group that hasn't been defined yet. In pattern2, group 2 does not exist. In pattern3 and pattern4, the back reference and capturing group are on different branches, making the back reference non-functional.
Trigger_Explanation: The JUnit test cases trigger the bug by calling the showBug method, which contains regex patterns with incorrect back references. The tests fail to indicate that the bug should be triggered, as the method attempts to compile these incorrect patterns.
